options: Identity theft (fraudulently using another's electronic signature or password)
explanation: Section 66C punishes whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person, with imprisonment up to 3 years and/or fine up to ₹1 lakh.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 66E of the IT Act, 2000 deals with:
options: Violation of privacy (capturing and publishing private area images)
explanation: Section 66E punishes whoever intentionally or knowingly captures, publishes or transmits the image of a private area of any person without consent, under circumstances violating the privacy of that person.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Under the IT Act 2000, the Adjudicating Officer has jurisdiction to adjudicate claims up to:
explanation: Section 46 empowers Adjudicating Officers to adjudicate whether any person has committed a contravention of the provisions of this Act — the pecuniary jurisdiction is up to ₹5 crore.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: The Cyber Appellate Tribunal (CAT) under the IT Act is established under:
explanation: Section 48 of the IT Act provides for the establishment of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals from orders of Adjudicating Officers under Section 46.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: An appeal against an order of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal under the IT Act lies to:
explanation: Section 62 of the IT Act provides that any person aggrieved by any decision or order of the Cyber Appellate Tribunal may file an appeal to the High Court within 60 days of the communication of the decision or order.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 72 of the IT Act, 2000 deals with:
explanation: Section 72 punishes any person who, in pursuance of any of the powers conferred under the Act, has secured access to any electronic record, book, register, etc., and discloses such information to any other person — breach of confidentiality and privacy.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 70 of the IT Act, 2000 deals with:
explanation: Section 70 empowers the Central Government to declare any computer resource as a 'protected system' and makes it an offence for any person to access or secure access to such protected system without authorisation.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 69 of the IT Act, 2000 empowers the government to:
options: Intercept, monitor, or decrypt any information
explanation: Section 69 empowers the Central Government or State Government to direct any agency to intercept, monitor, or decrypt or cause to be intercepted, monitored, or decrypted any information transmitted through any computer resource in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India, etc.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 empowers the government to:
options: Issue directions to block public access to information on specified grounds
explanation: Section 69A empowers the Central Government to direct any agency or intermediary to block access by the public to any information through any computer resource for reasons relating to sovereignty and integrity of India, defence, security, friendly relations with foreign states, or public order.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 (as read down in Shreya Singhal) provides:
options: Criminal liability for intermediaries for all third-party content
Mandatory monitoring of all online content by intermediaries
Strict liability for social media platforms
Safe harbour/exemption from liability for intermediaries if they comply with court/government takedown orders
explanation: Section 79 provides that an intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, provided certain conditions are met. After Shreya Singhal, intermediaries must act on court orders or government notifications to take down content.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 43 of the IT Act deals with:
options: Penalty and compensation for damage to computer systems (civil liability)
explanation: Section 43 provides civil remedies — if any person without permission of the owner of a computer resource accesses, downloads, introduces viruses, damages, or disrupts any computer, computer system, or network, he shall be liable to pay damages by way of compensation to the person so affected.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Section 43A of the IT Act (inserted 2008) deals with:
options: Compensation for failure to protect sensitive personal data
explanation: Section 43A holds body corporates that possess, deal or handle sensitive personal data or information liable to pay compensation to the affected person if they are negligent in maintaining reasonable security practices and procedures.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: The concept of 'chilling effect' on free speech, applied in Shreya Singhal, refers to:
options: The deterrent effect of vague/overbroad laws on legitimate speech
Physical harm caused to a person's reputation
The cooling-off period before filing a cyber complaint
explanation: The 'chilling effect' describes the inhibition or discouragement of the legitimate exercise of a fundamental right (especially free speech) caused by vague, overbroad, or disproportionate legal provisions.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Assertion (A): Section 66A of the IT Act, 2000 was struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). Reason (R): Section 66A was vague and overbroad, and fell outside the permissible restrictions on free speech under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: Both statements are correct. The Supreme Court struck down Section 66A precisely because it was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad, and the restrictions it imposed on speech were not saved by Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Assertion (A): An electronic record has the same legal validity as a paper document under the IT Act 2000. Reason (R): Section 4 of the IT Act gives legal recognition to electronic records, and Section 5 gives legal recognition to electronic signatures.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
explanation: Both statements are correct and the reason correctly explains the assertion. Sections 4 and 5 together provide the foundational legal recognition for electronic records and electronic signatures respectively, giving them the same validity as their paper/handwritten counterparts.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Under Section 67B, publishing child pornography in electronic form on first conviction is punishable by:
explanation: Section 67B prescribes punishment on first conviction of imprisonment up to 5 years and fine up to ₹10 lakh for publishing or transmitting material depicting children in sexually explicit act in electronic form.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: Match Section of IT Act with Subject Matter: (i) Section 43 → (ii) Section 66C → (iii) Section 66F → (iv) Section 67
options: i-Damage to computer systems (civil), ii-Identity theft, iii-Cyber terrorism, iv-Obscenity in electronic form
i-Cyber terrorism, ii-Damage to computer, iii-Obscenity, iv-Identity theft
i-Identity theft, ii-Obscenity, iii-Damage to computer, iv-Cyber terrorism
i-Obscenity, ii-Cyber terrorism, iii-Identity theft, iv-Damage to computer
explanation: Section 43 = civil penalty for damage to computer systems; Section 66C = identity theft; Section 66F = cyber terrorism (life imprisonment); Section 67 = publishing obscene material in electronic form.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: N - Cyber Crimes: Penalties and Adjudication
question: The correct appeal hierarchy under the IT Act 2000 is:
options: Cyber Appellate Tribunal → Adjudicating Officer → High Court
High Court → Adjudicating Officer → Cyber Appellate Tribunal
Adjudicating Officer → High Court → Supreme Court
Adjudicating Officer → Cyber Appellate Tribunal → High Court
explanation: The appeal hierarchy is: (1) Adjudicating Officer (Section 46); (2) Cyber Appellate Tribunal on appeal (Section 48/57); (3) High Court on further appeal (Section 62).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following pairs of IP rights does NOT require registration in India for the right to subsist?
explanation: Copyright (Section 13) and Performer's Rights (Section 38) arise automatically upon creation/performance without any requirement of registration. Patents, trademarks, GIs, and industrial designs all require registration.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The 'work for hire' doctrine in copyright, as reflected in Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957, provides that when an author creates a work under a contract of service or apprenticeship, the first owner of copyright is the:
options: Employer, in the absence of a contrary agreement
explanation: Section 17 provides that in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, where a work is made by an author in the course of his employment under a contract of service or apprenticeship, the employer shall be the first owner of the copyright therein.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which landmark case established that the 'sweat of the brow' doctrine does NOT apply in India and a higher threshold of creativity is required for copyright in compilations?
options: R.G. Anand v. M/s Deluxe Films (1978)
Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak (2008)
Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India (2005)
explanation: The Supreme Court in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak specifically rejected the 'sweat of the brow' doctrine (mere labour is insufficient) and held that a 'modicum of creativity' through the exercise of skill and judgment is required for copyright in compilations.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding copyright protection for computer programs in India?
options: Computer programs are protected as literary works under the Copyright Act, 1957
Computer programs are protected as artistic works
Computer programs have no IP protection in India
explanation: Section 2(o) of the Copyright Act defines 'literary work' to include computer programmes, tables and compilations including computer databases. Computer programs therefore receive copyright protection as literary works.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The Indian Patents Act, 1970 does NOT grant patent protection to:
explanation: Section 3(k) of the Patents Act specifically excludes computer programmes per se from patentable subject matter. Computer programs may be protected as literary works under copyright law.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The 'exhaustion of rights' doctrine (first-sale doctrine) in IP law means:
options: IP rights expire after a fixed period of use
IP rights are exhausted if not enforced within a limitation period
An IP owner must licence to all who request
Once the IP owner sells a product, they cannot control its subsequent resale
explanation: The exhaustion doctrine provides that once an IP owner sells a product, their IP rights in that specific product are 'exhausted' — they cannot prevent the buyer from reselling or using that particular item.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): Copyright in India does not require registration for subsistence of protection. Reason (R): India follows the Berne Convention principle of automatic protection upon creation.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
explanation: Both are correct. India follows the Berne Convention's automatic protection principle — copyright subsists as soon as the original work is created and fixed in a material form, without requiring any formality such as registration.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): Section 3(d) of the Patents Act 1970 prevents grant of patent to new forms of known substances unless enhanced efficacy is demonstrated. Reason (R): This provision is aimed at preventing 'evergreening' of pharmaceutical patents.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: Both are correct and the reason correctly explains the purpose of Section 3(d). By requiring enhanced efficacy, the provision prevents pharmaceutical companies from obtaining new patents on minor modifications of existing drugs (evergreening) to artificially extend their monopoly.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): Traditional Knowledge (TK) cannot be protected as a patent in India. Reason (R): Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes inventions which are traditional knowledge or aggregation/duplication of known properties of traditionally known components.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: Both are correct. Section 3(p) specifically excludes traditional knowledge from patentability, thereby providing a statutory basis for the protection of India's traditional knowledge against biopiracy.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Under the Berne Convention, which principle removes the need for any formalities (registration, deposit) as a condition for copyright protection?
explanation: Article 5(2) of the Berne Convention establishes the principle that the enjoyment and the exercise of copyright shall not be subject to any formality — protection is automatic upon creation of the work.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following correctly reflects the hierarchy of IP appeal authorities in India for patent matters (post-2021)?
options: Patent Office → District Court → High Court → Supreme Court
Controller General → Cyber Appellate Tribunal → High Court
Patent Office → High Court → Supreme Court
explanation: The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021. Appeals from orders of the Controller (Patent Office) now lie directly to the High Court, and further appeals lie to the Supreme Court.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): India's TKDL (Traditional Knowledge Digital Library) acts as a 'defensive' form of traditional knowledge protection. Reason (R): TKDL does not grant exclusive IP rights to TK holders; instead, it creates prior art databases to prevent third parties from obtaining patents over traditional knowledge.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: Both are correct. TKDL is a defensive protection mechanism — it does not create any new IP rights in traditional knowledge; instead it serves as a prior art database accessible to patent examiners worldwide, preventing third parties from obtaining patents on traditional Indian knowledge.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following statements about the TRIPS Agreement is INCORRECT?
options: It is administered exclusively by WIPO
It sets minimum standards of IP protection for WTO members
It provides for enforcement of IP rights
explanation: TRIPS is administered by the WTO (World Trade Organization), not by WIPO. While WIPO administers most IP conventions (Berne, Paris, PCT etc.), TRIPS is an agreement under the WTO framework.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): India's sui generis plant variety protection system under the PPV&FR Act, 2001 is more balanced than the UPOV model. Reason (R): Unlike UPOV, the Indian Act incorporates farmers' rights, allowing farmers to save, use, exchange, and sell farm-saved seed (but not branded seed) of protected varieties, thereby protecting food security and traditional agricultural practices.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: Both are correct. The PPV&FR Act is widely regarded as more balanced than UPOV because it explicitly protects farmers' rights — including the right to save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share or sell farm produce of protected varieties — a dimension absent from UPOV.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Consider the following statements about patentability under the Patents Act, 1970, and identify which are CORRECT: (i) A new use of a known substance is patentable without showing enhanced efficacy. (ii) Methods of agriculture are not patentable. (iii) Mathematical methods are not patentable. (iv) Living micro-organisms produced by human intervention can be patentable.
explanation: Statement (i) is incorrect — Section 3(d) prevents patenting new uses of known substances without proof of enhanced efficacy. Statements (ii), (iii), and (iv) are correct: Section 3(h) excludes agriculture/horticulture; Section 3(k) excludes mathematical methods; and micro-organisms with technical application may be patentable (unlike plants/animals under Section 3(j)).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between copyright and the Internet in India?
options: The IT Act, 2000 entirely governs copyright on the Internet
The Copyright Act, 1957 (as amended in 2012) applies to digital content; the IT Act governs electronic records and cyber offences; both operate concurrently
Neither the Copyright Act nor the IT Act applies to Internet content
WIPO directly governs copyright disputes on Indian websites
explanation: In India, copyright in digital content is governed by the Copyright Act, 1957 (aligned with WIPO Internet Treaties through the 2012 amendment), while cyber offences relating to IP (digital piracy as a cyber crime, circumvention of technical protection measures, etc.) are also addressed under the IT Act, 2000. Both statutes operate concurrently.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Consider the following statements about the Designs Act, 2000 and the Copyright Act, 1957 and identify the CORRECT statement:
options: A design registered under the Designs Act continues to enjoy copyright protection after the design's registration term expires
A design capable of being registered under the Designs Act but which has NOT been registered does not lose copyright protection until industrially reproduced more than 50 times
Designs Act and Copyright Act operate in completely separate spheres with no overlap
Any artistic work automatically gets design protection without registration
explanation: Section 15(2) of the Copyright Act provides that copyright in an artistic work (which is capable of being registered as a design but has not been so registered) ceases once the article to which the design has been applied has been reproduced more than fifty times by an industrial process. Until that threshold, copyright is retained.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following correctly states the three objectives of the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, 1992)?
options: Conservation of biological diversity, sustainable use of its components, and fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from genetic resources
Patenting of biological resources, sustainable use, and commercialisation
Conservation, prohibition on use, and regulation of GMOs
Biodiversity conservation, prevention of biopiracy, and free access to genetic resources
explanation: Article 1 of the CBD states its three objectives: (1) conservation of biological diversity; (2) the sustainable use of its components; and (3) the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising out of the utilisation of genetic resources.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The 'Digital piracy' in the context of copyright means:
options: Unauthorised copying, distribution, or downloading of copyrighted works in digital form
explanation: Digital piracy refers to the unauthorised reproduction, distribution, or use of copyrighted material in digital format, including movies, music, software, and books, through the internet or other digital means.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): A geographical indication tag cannot be used as a generic term in trade. Reason (R): Once a GI is registered, it cannot be used to indicate a type or style of product; it must identify the specific geographical origin from which the product derives its qualities.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
Both A and R are incorrect
explanation: A registered GI cannot become generic — the GI Act and TRIPS prevent a GI from being used to designate a variety, type, or style of product without reference to the specific geographical region from which the product originates.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which combination correctly represents the THREE pillars of patentability?
explanation: Under Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970, an 'invention' must satisfy three criteria: (1) Novelty — it must be new; (2) Inventive Step — it must not be obvious (non-obvious); and (3) Industrial Application — it must be capable of being made or used in industry.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following is the MOST ACCURATE statement about moral rights under copyright?
options: Moral rights are economic rights that can be freely assigned
Moral rights survive assignment of copyright and are inalienable under Section 57 of the Copyright Act
Moral rights are only available to the publisher of a work
Moral rights expire with the economic term of copyright
explanation: Section 57 of the Copyright Act grants authors the right of paternity (attribution) and the right of integrity. These rights are personal rights of the author, survive the assignment of copyright to another person, are inalienable, and exist even after the author's death.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: In copyright law, what does the term 'neighbouring rights' (or 'related rights') refer to?
options: Rights of persons who live near the copyright holder
Rights of performers, producers of phonograms, and broadcasting organisations — distinct from but related to copyright
Rights of the heirs and successors of the copyright holder
Rights of co-authors who contributed to a joint work
explanation: Neighbouring rights (related rights) are rights accorded to performers, producers of phonograms, and broadcasting organisations. They are distinct from copyright (which protects authors) but are 'neighbouring' in the sense that they protect persons who disseminate or perform creative works.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 establishes which three-tier structure?
options: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) → State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) → Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs)
National Biodiversity Authority → Central Biodiversity Board → Regional Committees
Ministry of Environment → State Pollution Boards → District Committees
explanation: The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 creates a three-tier structure: (1) National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) at the national level; (2) State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) at the state level; and (3) Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) at the local level, typically at panchayat/municipality level.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which provision of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with 'inventive step' (non-obviousness)?
explanation: Section 2(1)(ja) of the Patents Act defines 'inventive step' as a feature of an invention that involves technical advance as compared to the existing knowledge or having economic significance or both and that makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: What is the correct definition of 'trade mark' under Section 2(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999?
options: Any symbol used in commerce to identify a product
Only word marks and logos registered with the Trade Marks Registry
A mark capable of being represented graphically and capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others
Any distinctive sign used by a manufacturer
explanation: Section 2(zb) defines 'trade mark' as a mark capable of being represented graphically and which is capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one person from those of others and may include shape of goods, their packaging, and combination of colours.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Under the IT Amendment Act 2008, Section 66D deals with:
options: Cheating by impersonation using a computer resource
explanation: Section 66D punishes whoever, by means of any communication device or computer resource, cheats by personation — i.e., assumes the identity of another person to deceive someone — with imprisonment up to 3 years and/or fine up to ₹1 lakh.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following is NOT an absolute ground for refusal of trademark registration under Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999?
options: A mark which is similar to an earlier registered trademark for similar goods
A mark which is devoid of distinctive character
A mark which consists exclusively of signs designating quality of the goods
A mark which is contrary to public morality
explanation: Similarity to an earlier registered trademark is a relative ground for refusal under Section 11, not an absolute ground under Section 9. Absolute grounds relate to the mark's inherent registrability regardless of other marks.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: In India, which authority administers and controls the Patent Office, Trade Marks Registry, GI Registry, and Designs Wing?
options: Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry
explanation: The Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM), functioning under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, administers the Patent Office, Trade Marks Registry, GI Registry, and Designs Wing.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Section 67A of the IT Act, 2000 deals with punishment for:
options: Publishing or transmitting sexually explicit material in electronic form
explanation: Section 67A, inserted by the IT (Amendment) Act 2008, punishes whoever publishes or transmits material containing sexually explicit act in electronic form with imprisonment up to 5 years and fine up to ₹10 lakh on first conviction.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: The IT (Amendment) Act, 2008 came into force on:
explanation: The Information Technology (Amendment) Act, 2008, which received Presidential assent on 5 February 2009, came into force on the same date — 5 February 2009.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following transactions is EXCLUDED from the application of the IT Act, 2000?
options: Sale of immovable property through electronic record
explanation: The First Schedule to the IT Act lists exclusions including: negotiable instruments (other than cheques), powers of attorney, trusts, wills, and any contract for the sale or conveyance of immovable property or any interest in such property.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Section 72A of the IT Act, 2000 deals with:
options: Breach of confidentiality by government officials
Disclosure of information in breach of a lawful contract
explanation: Section 72A punishes any person including an intermediary who, while providing services under the terms of lawful contract, has secured access to any material containing personal information about another person, and without the consent of the person concerned, discloses such material to any other person.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Domain name disputes in India relating to well-known trademarks are governed primarily through:
options: Trade Marks Act, 1999 and the doctrine of passing off
explanation: Domain name disputes in India are primarily resolved through the Trade Marks Act, 1999 (for registered marks) and the common law action of passing off (for unregistered marks with established goodwill), as established in cases like Yahoo Inc. v. Akash Arora.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Assertion (A): Copyright in India does not require registration for subsistence of protection. Reason (R): The Berne Convention (to which India is a member) establishes the principle that enjoyment and exercise of copyright shall not be subject to any formality.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
explanation: India is a signatory to the Berne Convention. Article 5(2) of the Berne Convention prohibits member states from imposing formalities (registration, deposit, etc.) as a condition for copyright protection — this principle is reflected in the Copyright Act, 1957.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Which of the following is the correct meaning of 'biopiracy' in the context of intellectual property?
options: Appropriation of biological resources or traditional knowledge of indigenous communities without fair compensation or acknowledgment
explanation: Biopiracy refers to the appropriation of the genetic resources and traditional knowledge of indigenous and local communities for commercial purposes without obtaining prior informed consent or sharing benefits equitably with the source communities.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: O - Advanced Integrated and Case-Law Based Questions
question: Under the Patents Act, 1970, who may apply for a patent?
options: Any person claiming to be the true and first inventor or their assignee, including foreign nationals
explanation: Section 6 of the Patents Act provides that an application for a patent may be made by any person claiming to be the true and first inventor of the invention, or the assignee of such person, or the legal representative of a deceased person. There is no restriction on nationality.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property was signed in:
explanation: The Paris Convention was signed on 20 March 1883 and is the foundational international treaty for industrial property protection.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works was adopted in:
explanation: The Berne Convention was adopted on 9 September 1886 in Berne, Switzerland. It is the primary international instrument for copyright protection.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Madrid Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Marks was signed in:
explanation: The Madrid Agreement was signed on 14 April 1891, establishing the Madrid System for international registration of trademarks.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) was concluded in:
explanation: The Patent Cooperation Treaty was done at Washington on 19 June 1970 and entered into force on 24 January 1978.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Convention Establishing the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) was signed in:
explanation: The WIPO Convention was signed at Stockholm on 14 July 1967 and entered into force in 1970.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Microorganisms for the Purposes of Patent Procedure was concluded in:
explanation: The Budapest Treaty was done at Budapest on 28 April 1977 and entered into force on 19 August 1980.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Nairobi Treaty on the Protection of the Olympic Symbol was adopted in:
explanation: The Nairobi Treaty was adopted on 26 September 1981 at Nairobi, Kenya. It protects the Olympic symbol (five interlaced rings) against commercial exploitation without authorisation of the IOC.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Rome Convention for the Protection of Performers, Producers of Phonograms and Broadcasting Organizations was adopted in:
explanation: The Rome Convention was adopted on 26 October 1961 at Rome, Italy. It is the foundational treaty for neighbouring (related) rights.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Geneva Convention for the Protection of Producers of Phonograms Against Unauthorized Duplication of Their Phonograms was concluded in:
explanation: The Geneva Phonograms Convention was done at Geneva on 29 October 1971.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Brussels Convention Relating to the Distribution of Programme-Carrying Signals Transmitted by Satellite was concluded in:
explanation: The Brussels Satellite Convention was concluded on 21 May 1974 at Brussels. It deals with the protection of signals transmitted by satellite against unauthorized distribution.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The WIPO Copyright Treaty (WCT) and the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty (WPPT) were both adopted in:
explanation: Both the WCT and WPPT were adopted at the WIPO Diplomatic Conference in Geneva on 20 December 1996. They are known as the 'WIPO Internet Treaties'.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The TRIPS Agreement entered into force as part of the WTO framework in:
explanation: Though signed in April 1994 at Marrakesh, TRIPS entered into force on 1 January 1995 when the WTO Agreement came into force.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Hague Agreement Concerning the International Registration of Industrial Designs (Geneva Act) was adopted in:
explanation: The Geneva Act of the Hague Agreement was adopted on 2 July 1999. It is the most recent and widely used act of the Hague System for international design registration.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health was adopted in:
explanation: The Doha Declaration was adopted at the Fourth WTO Ministerial Conference at Doha, Qatar on 14 November 2001.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances was adopted in:
explanation: The Beijing Treaty on Audiovisual Performances was adopted at the WIPO Diplomatic Conference in Beijing on 26 June 2012.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Marrakesh Treaty to Facilitate Access to Published Works for Persons Who Are Blind, Visually Impaired, or Otherwise Print Disabled was adopted in:
explanation: The Marrakesh Treaty was adopted on 27 June 2013 at Marrakesh, Morocco. It entered into force on 30 September 2016.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce was adopted in:
explanation: The UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce was adopted by the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) in 1996 (resolution 51/162 of the UN General Assembly).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in:
explanation: The CBD was opened for signature at the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED / Rio Earth Summit) in Rio de Janeiro in June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing (under CBD) was adopted in:
explanation: The Nagoya Protocol was adopted at the 10th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the CBD (COP-10) in Nagoya, Japan in October 2010 and entered into force in 2014.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Madrid Protocol Concerning the International Registration of Marks was adopted in:
explanation: The Protocol Relating to the Madrid Agreement was adopted at Madrid on 27 June 1989. Unlike the Madrid Agreement (1891), the Protocol is more flexible and has wider membership including the USA, EU, Japan, and India.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Washington Treaty on Intellectual Property in Respect of Integrated Circuits was adopted in:
explanation: The Washington Treaty (IPIC Treaty) was adopted on 26 May 1989 at Washington D.C. It never came into force, but its substantive provisions were incorporated into TRIPS Article 35.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: India ratified the Madrid Protocol for International Trademark Registration in:
explanation: India acceded to the Madrid Protocol on 8 April 2013, enabling Indian trademark applicants to file a single application to seek trademark protection in multiple member countries.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The UPOV Convention (International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants) was first adopted in:
explanation: The UPOV Convention was adopted on 2 December 1961 at Paris. It has been revised in 1972, 1978, and 1991. India is not a member of UPOV.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Nice Agreement Concerning the International Classification of Goods and Services for the Purposes of the Registration of Marks was concluded in:
explanation: The Nice Agreement was concluded on 15 June 1957 at Nice, France. It establishes a classification system (Nice Classification) for goods and services used for trademark registration worldwide — currently comprising 45 classes.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Vienna Agreement Establishing an International Classification of the Figurative Elements of Marks was concluded in:
explanation: The Vienna Agreement was concluded on 12 June 1973 at Vienna, Austria. It establishes a classification system (Vienna Classification) for the figurative elements of marks.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Locarno Agreement Establishing an International Classification for Industrial Designs was concluded in:
explanation: The Locarno Agreement was concluded on 8 October 1968 at Locarno, Switzerland. It establishes an international classification system (Locarno Classification) for industrial designs.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Strasbourg Agreement Concerning the International Patent Classification (IPC) was concluded in:
explanation: The Strasbourg Agreement was concluded on 24 March 1971 at Strasbourg. It establishes the International Patent Classification (IPC) system used by patent offices worldwide to classify patent documents.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Lisbon Agreement for the Protection of Appellations of Origin and their International Registration was concluded in:
explanation: The Lisbon Agreement was concluded on 31 October 1958 at Lisbon, Portugal. It established the Lisbon System for the international registration of appellations of origin (a form of geographical indication).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: The Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement on Appellations of Origin and Geographical Indications was adopted in:
explanation: The Geneva Act of the Lisbon Agreement was adopted on 20 May 2015. It modernised the Lisbon System, extending it to cover geographical indications in addition to appellations of origin.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: P - Conventions & Treaties: Year-Based Memory Questions
question: Which convention first introduced the 'right of priority' as a concept in international IP law?
explanation: The Paris Convention (1883) was the first to introduce the right of priority — allowing an applicant who has filed for IP protection in one member country to claim the same filing date (priority date) in other member countries within specified periods.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: India's first patent legislation was the:
explanation: The Patents and Designs Act, 1911 was India's first comprehensive legislation covering both patents and designs. It was replaced by the Patents Act, 1970 (for patents) and the Designs Act, 2000 (for designs).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 was replaced by the Trade Marks Act in:
explanation: The Trade Marks Act, 1999 replaced the Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958 to bring Indian trademark law in conformity with TRIPS and international practices.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Designs Act, 2000 replaced which earlier legislation?
options: The Trade and Merchandise Marks Act, 1958
explanation: The Designs Act, 2000 replaced Part II of the Patents and Designs Act, 1911, which had earlier governed industrial design protection in India.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 and the Trade Marks Act, 1999 both came into force on the same date, which was:
explanation: Both the GI Act, 1999 and the Trade Marks Act, 1999 came into force simultaneously on 15 September 2003.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act was enacted in:
explanation: The Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act was enacted in 2001 and came into force in 2005 with the establishment of the PPV&FRA.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act was enacted in:
explanation: The Semiconductor Integrated Circuits Layout-Design Act, 2000 was enacted to comply with Part II, Section 6 of the TRIPS Agreement on layout-designs (topographies) of integrated circuits.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Intellectual Property Appellate Board (IPAB) was abolished in:
explanation: The IPAB was abolished by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021. Its jurisdiction over patents, trademarks, GIs, and copyright was transferred to the respective High Courts.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: India became a member of the Paris Convention in:
explanation: India acceded to the Paris Convention on 7 December 1998. (Note: Some sources cite earlier membership; the key fact for exams is that India is a member and the TRIPS-era re-accession for compliance purposes.)

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Copyright Act, 1957 replaced which earlier legislation?
explanation: The Copyright Act, 1957 replaced the Indian Copyright Act, 1914 which was based on the British Copyright Act, 1911.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: Q - Indian IP Legislation: Key Dates and Historical Facts
question: The Patents Act, 1970 came into force (most provisions) in:
explanation: Although enacted in 1970, the Patents Act came into force on 20 April 1972.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under the Patents Act 1970, Section 2(1)(j) defines:
explanation: Section 2(1)(j) defines 'invention' as a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 2(1)(ja) of the Patents Act, 1970 defines:
explanation: Section 2(1)(ja), inserted by the 2002 amendment, defines 'inventive step' as a feature of an invention that involves technical advance as compared to existing knowledge or economic significance and makes the invention not obvious to a person skilled in the art.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 25 of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with:
options: Revocation of patent by the High Court
explanation: Section 25 provides for opposition to grant of patent — Section 25(1) deals with pre-grant opposition (any person may oppose before grant) and Section 25(2) deals with post-grant opposition (any interested person may oppose within 12 months of publication of grant).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 39 of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with:
options: Government's right to use an invention
Residents not to apply for patents outside India without prior permission
explanation: Section 39 prohibits a person resident in India from making an application for a patent outside India without first filing an application in India and obtaining prior permission of the Controller, unless 6 weeks have elapsed since Indian filing.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 100 of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with:
options: Power of Central Government to use inventions for purposes of government
explanation: Section 100 empowers the Central Government to use any patented invention for the purposes of the government at any time after the patent has been granted, subject to payment of adequate remuneration to the patentee.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under the Trade Marks Act 1999, Section 9 deals with:
options: Absolute grounds for refusal of registration
explanation: Section 9 of the Trade Marks Act sets out the absolute grounds for refusal of registration — these are intrinsic defects in the mark itself, such as lack of distinctiveness, descriptiveness, deceptiveness, or being contrary to public morality.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under the Trade Marks Act 1999, Section 11 deals with:
options: Relative grounds for refusal of registration
explanation: Section 11 of the Trade Marks Act sets out the relative grounds for refusal — these arise when the mark is similar or identical to an earlier trademark for similar or identical goods/services causing likelihood of confusion.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 deals with:
explanation: Section 29 defines the acts that constitute infringement of a registered trademark, including use of an identical/similar mark for identical/similar goods/services without the consent of the registered proprietor.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 134 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 deals with:
options: Jurisdiction of courts in suits for infringement
explanation: Section 134 provides that no suit for infringement of trademark or passing off shall be instituted in any court inferior to a District Court having jurisdiction to try the suit. It also provides for special jurisdiction — suit may be filed where the plaintiff resides/carries on business.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: The term 'copyright' in the Copyright Act 1957 is defined in Section:
explanation: Section 14 of the Copyright Act defines 'copyright' by enumerating the exclusive rights that the copyright owner has in respect of each category of work (literary, dramatic, musical, artistic, film, sound recording).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: The term 'author' in relation to a cinematograph film under the Copyright Act 1957 means:
explanation: Section 2(d)(v) of the Copyright Act defines 'author' in relation to a cinematograph film as the producer of the film.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: The term 'author' in relation to a sound recording under the Copyright Act 1957 means:
options: The producer of the sound recording
explanation: Section 2(d)(vi) defines 'author' in relation to any sound recording as the producer of the sound recording.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under Section 22 of the Copyright Act 1957, the term of copyright for a literary work is:
options: 60 years from the year of publication
explanation: Section 22 provides that the term of copyright for literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works shall subsist until 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year next following the year in which the author dies.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under which Section of the Copyright Act 1957 does the government hold copyright in government works?
explanation: Section 17(dd) (as amended) provides that in the case of a work made or published by or under the direction or control of any public undertaking, the public undertaking shall be the first owner of copyright. Government works are covered by proviso (a) to Section 17.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 16 of the Copyright Act, 1957 embodies which important doctrine?
explanation: Section 16 provides that no person shall be entitled to copyright or any similar right in any work otherwise than under and in accordance with the provisions of this Act — impliedly codifying that copyright does not protect ideas, only their specific expression.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Section 31C of the Copyright Act (inserted 2012) deals with:
options: Statutory licence for cover versions of musical works
explanation: Section 31C provides for statutory licence for cover versions — any person may make a cover version of a sound recording of any literary or musical work after 5 years from the year of first publication, on payment of royalties.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under the GI Act 1999, the term of registration of a geographical indication is:
explanation: Under the GI Act, 1999, the period of registration of a geographical indication is 10 years and it may be renewed from time to time for periods of 10 years each.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under the GI Act 1999, who can file an application for registration of a GI?
options: Any association of persons, producers, organisation or authority established by law
explanation: Section 11 of the GI Act allows any association of persons or producers or any organisation or authority established by or under any law for the time being in force representing the interest of the producers of the concerned goods to apply for GI registration.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: R - Specific Sections and Provisions (Memory-Based)
question: Under Section 84(1) of the Patents Act 1970, which of the following is NOT a ground for compulsory licensing?
options: Reasonable requirements of the public not satisfied
Patented invention not available at a reasonably affordable price
Patented invention not worked in India
explanation: Fraudulent procurement of a patent is a ground for revocation under Section 64, not compulsory licensing under Section 84. The three grounds for compulsory licensing under Section 84 are: (a) public requirements not satisfied; (b) not available at reasonably affordable price; (c) not worked in India.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: In which year did the Supreme Court of India decide Novartis AG v. Union of India (Section 3(d) case)?
explanation: The Supreme Court of India decided Novartis AG v. Union of India on 1 April 2013, upholding Section 3(d) of the Patents Act and refusing the patent for the beta-crystalline form of Imatinib Mesylate (Gleevec).

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, striking down Section 66A of the IT Act, was decided in:
explanation: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India was decided by the Supreme Court on 24 March 2015.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak, rejecting the 'sweat of the brow' doctrine, was given in:
explanation: Eastern Book Company v. D.B. Modak was decided by the Supreme Court of India in 2008.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The Delhi High Court recognised and enforced moral rights of a sculptor under Section 57 of the Copyright Act in the case of Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India in:
explanation: Amar Nath Sehgal v. Union of India was decided by the Delhi High Court in 2005. The court awarded damages for destruction of the sculptor's mural and recognised the right of integrity under Section 57.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The Supreme Court decided N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool Corporation (transborder reputation case) in:
explanation: N.R. Dongre v. Whirlpool Corporation was decided by the Supreme Court in 1996, establishing that a mark with transborder reputation can be protected in India even without prior use in India.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The Delhi High Court decided Yahoo Inc. v. Akash Arora (India's first cybersquatting case) in:
explanation: Yahoo Inc. v. Akash Arora was decided by the Delhi High Court in 1999. It was India's first major domain name/cybersquatting dispute.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The R.G. Anand v. Deluxe Films case on idea-expression dichotomy was decided by the Supreme Court in:
explanation: R.G. Anand v. M/s Deluxe Films & Ors. was decided by the Supreme Court in 1978. It remains the leading Indian authority on the idea-expression dichotomy in copyright law.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: The US Supreme Court decided Diamond v. Chakrabarty (living organisms as patentable subject matter) in:
explanation: Diamond v. Chakrabarty was decided by the US Supreme Court in 1980. The court held (5-4) that a live, human-made microorganism is patentable subject matter.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: S - Case Laws: Year and Holding (Memory-Based)
question: India's first compulsory licence (Natco v. Bayer, for Nexavar/Sorafenib) was granted by the Patent Controller in:
explanation: The Patent Controller granted India's first compulsory licence to Natco Pharma Ltd. for Sorafenib Tosylate (Nexavar) on 9 March 2012.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: T - Missed Aspects: Licensing, Assignment, Remedies, Special Topics
question: Under the Patents Act 1970, the term 'voluntary licence' refers to:
options: A licence granted by the patentee to another person by agreement
A licence granted by the government without the patent owner's consent
A licence automatically granted upon expiry of patent term
A licence granted by the Controller under Section 84
explanation: A voluntary licence under the Patents Act is a contractual arrangement where the patentee (licensor) grants permission to another person (licensee) to make, use, or sell the patented invention on agreed terms and conditions.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: T - Missed Aspects: Licensing, Assignment, Remedies, Special Topics
question: Which of the following correctly describes a 'licence of right' under the Patents Act, 1970?
options: A licence granted by the patent owner without any conditions
A licence granted as of right to any person who applies, after endorsement by the Controller
explanation: Under Section 87, where a patent has been endorsed 'licences of right', any person who desires to work the patented invention may apply to the patentee for a licence — the patentee cannot refuse without cause, and disputes go to the Controller.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: T - Missed Aspects: Licensing, Assignment, Remedies, Special Topics
question: Which of the following is TRUE about the assignment of a patent in India?
options: Assignment of a patent must be in writing
A patent can be assigned orally
Assignment requires approval of the Controller
A patent cannot be assigned under Indian law
explanation: Section 68 of the Patents Act provides that an assignment of a patent or of a share in a patent, a mortgage, licence, or the creation of any other interest in a patent shall not be valid unless the same were in writing and the agreement between the parties concerned is reduced to the form of a document embodying all the terms and conditions.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: T - Missed Aspects: Licensing, Assignment, Remedies, Special Topics
question: The 'doctrine of colourable imitation' in trademark law means:
options: Using identical colours in a competing trademark
Deliberately copying a competitor's colour scheme
Making a mark so similar to a registered mark that it is likely to deceive consumers
Using a similar sounding name for a competing product
explanation: Colourable imitation means a mark that so nearly resembles an existing registered mark as to be likely to deceive or cause confusion — it is a slightly altered version of the original mark designed to escape literal copying while still misleading consumers.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law
topic: T - Missed Aspects: Licensing, Assignment, Remedies, Special Topics
question: The principle of 'functionality' in design and trademark law provides that:
options: Functional features of a product are always protectable as trademarks
Only functional designs can be registered
Functional marks get stronger protection than non-functional marks
Functional features of a product cannot receive trademark or design protection
explanation: The functionality doctrine prevents the use of trademark or design law to protect utilitarian/functional features of a product — such features must be protected through patent law (if at all), not through trademark or design registration.

subject: Intellectual Property Rights and Information Technology Law

question: Under TRIPS Article 27(2), member states may exclude from patentability inventions whose commercial exploitation would be contrary to:
explanation: TRIPS Article 27(2) allows member states to exclude from patentability inventions whose prevention within their territory of the commercial exploitation of which is necessary to protect ordre public or morality, including to protect human, animal or plant life or health or to avoid serious prejudice to the environment.

question: The concept of 'orphan works' in copyright law refers to:
options: Works that are still under copyright but whose owners cannot be identified or located
Works that have never been published
explanation: Orphan works are copyrighted works whose rights holders cannot be identified or found, making it difficult for potential users to obtain permissions. They represent a significant barrier to digitisation and access to cultural heritage.

question: The 'three-step test' under TRIPS (Article 13) for copyright exceptions allows exceptions only if they:
options: Are limited to certain special cases, do not conflict with normal exploitation of the work, and do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the rights holder
Are explicitly listed in national legislation
explanation: The three-step test (originally in Berne Convention Article 9(2), incorporated in TRIPS Article 13) permits copyright exceptions/limitations only if: (1) they are confined to certain special cases; (2) do not conflict with normal exploitation of the work; and (3) do not unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the author.

question: Under the Copyright Act 1957, a 'licence' of copyright is different from 'assignment' because:
options: A licence transfers ownership; assignment does not
An assignment transfers ownership of copyright; a licence only grants permission to use without transfer of ownership
A licence must be registered; an assignment need not be
explanation: An assignment (Section 18-19) transfers the ownership of copyright itself to the assignee. A licence (Section 30) merely grants permission to the licensee to exercise certain rights — the copyright remains with the licensor.

Importing goods under a compulsory licence
explanation: Parallel importation involves importing genuine (not counterfeit) goods that have been placed on the market in another country by or with the consent of the rights holder. Whether this is permitted depends on which exhaustion regime (national/regional/international) a country adopts.

explanation: The Doctrine of Pith and Marrow (used in UK/Indian patent law, analogous to the US doctrine of equivalents) identifies the essential integers of a patent claim — if an alleged infringer takes all the essential elements (the pith and marrow) of the patent, infringement is established even without literal copying of every claim element.

question: A 'patent troll' or 'Non-Practicing Entity (NPE)' in IP law refers to:
options: A government body that administers patents
A person who files fraudulent patent applications
A company that files for multiple patents on the same invention
An entity that acquires patents primarily to assert them against alleged infringers rather than to manufacture or commercialise products
explanation: Patent trolls (NPEs) are entities that hold patents not to manufacture products but primarily to collect licensing fees or sue for infringement. They are a subject of significant controversy in patent policy.

explanation: Section 47 of the Trade Marks Act provides that a registered trademark may be removed from the register on the ground that it was registered without any bona fide intention to use it, or that it has not been used for a continuous period of 5 years and 3 months before the date of application for removal.

question: The 'Doctrine of Colourable Variation' in patent law provides that:
options: Patents must describe their colour requirements
Colour cannot be patented as a design element
A trivial or immaterial variation from a patented invention does not avoid infringement
A patent may be varied by the Controller on application
explanation: The doctrine of colourable variation holds that making a trivial or inconsequential change to a patented invention to escape literal infringement is not sufficient — such a colourable variation still constitutes infringement if the essential features of the invention are taken.

options: Trade secrets must inevitably be disclosed in patent applications
Trade secrets disclosed in court proceedings lose protection
An employer must inevitably share trade secrets with employees
A former employee will inevitably disclose trade secrets in a new job, justifying a court injunction even without proof of actual misappropriation
explanation: The Doctrine of Inevitable Disclosure (primarily a US concept, also discussed in Indian trade secret contexts) allows an employer to prevent a former employee from working for a competitor if the new job would inevitably require disclosure of the former employer's trade secrets.

The licensee must pay no royalties
Compulsory licences must be granted for all patented inventions simultaneously
No conditions apply in national emergencies
explanation: TRIPS Article 31 requires that before a compulsory licence is granted, the potential user must have first made efforts to obtain authorisation from the rights holder on reasonable commercial terms, and such efforts have not been successful within a reasonable period. This requirement may be waived in national emergencies.

options: A work that is entirely copied from another
A work made by an employee for an employer
A work that has entered the public domain
A work based upon one or more pre-existing works, such as a translation, musical arrangement, dramatisation, or adaptation
explanation: A derivative work is one that is based upon one or more existing works and incorporates creative expression from those works. Examples include translations, adaptations, dramatisations, abridgements, and motion picture versions of novels. Creating a derivative work requires the permission of the original copyright holder.

Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, 1996
explanation: Section 512 of the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), 1998 provides the 'safe harbour' provisions for ISPs limiting their liability for copyright infringement by users, provided they comply with notice-and-takedown procedures.
